item.title: Tracker: Who counts? A ledger of how AI is checked

item.title: Thread: The wave and the leash
item.description: Who should count the failures when people hand more of what they do to AI, and how can anyone tell that the counting is independent of the thing being counted? An essay on the long line of capacities people have handed to tools and institutions, why most of us will not refuse the next handoff to AI, and who should independently count its failures. Includes Who counts?, a quarterly ledger of how AI is being checked.

item.title: Essay: The wave and the leash
item.description: People have always handed parts of their lives to things bigger and faster than any one of us. AI may be the first handoff to reach the whole loop of sensing, remembering, learning, deciding and acting. Most people will not refuse it, so the practical question is who counts its failures, independently of the thing counted.

item.title: Podcast: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: Jev from TypeSafe AI answers a defined question about text with a probability. What happens when researchers put this unusual tool through cognitive tests designed for people? This short conversation follows the independent work on xanderpico.com: a trait-order result opposite to the first-impression pattern used for comparison, a conjunction judgment that changes with layout, and word-similarity rankings that resemble human ratings while the raw scores do not. The hosts turn those results into practical advice for builders: pin the version and exact question, test wording, order and layout, compare with human ratings where available, and keep inactive inputs separate. The article and linked result write-ups have the full methods, numbers and caveats. Independent work; not affiliated with or endorsed by TypeSafe. This episode uses scripted AI-generated hosts and synthetic voices.

item.title: Podcast: Frontier labs as national laboratories, the October newsletter
item.description: Frontier AI labs already get lab-style treatment from the US government, but through one-off levers rather than the contract that makes national labs open, graded and replaceable. This episode walks through the October issue of the Frontier Labs newsletter on xanderpico.com: the six levers in use, estimates for nine paths to 2030, the strongest objection, and what to watch next. Every claim comes from the published newsletter, which lists all 37 sources. The hosts, George and Jessica, are AI voices.

item.title: Thread: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: Where do the quick judgments of a very cheap AI differ from ours, and what does running thousands of tests teach us about minds and about building with AI? Jev, from TypeSafe AI, answers a typed question about a text with a probability in about a fifth of a second for about two thousandths of a cent, and when it is confident it gives the same answer each time. That makes psychology-style experiments practical at a scale that normally needs hundreds of volunteers: rating thousands of words, or running a battery of classic bias tests in minutes. What turns up matters to AI builders, Jev users and brain researchers: some human quirks appear, some do not, and on first impressions it does the opposite of people.

item.title: Results: Rating words the way people do
item.category: Cognitive tests at scale, for pennies
item.description: A cheap AI model rates 400 words each for concreteness, valence and arousal and is compared with published human norms: close on two, weaker on arousal, and where it disagrees. Work in progress.

item.title: Thread: Scale Tool
item.description: What can a single number mean when it is compared, without false equivalence, across quantities such as time, distance, mass, energy, information, and temperature? A React and TypeScript explorer in which one editable decimal value drives source-backed comparisons across nine distinct units. It keeps estimates, models, theory, and unknown quantities explicitly separate from measurements.

item.title: Thread: Jev Turing
item.description: What can be learned by treating one probabilistic, typed AI judgment as a logic primitive and checking each result against a known Boolean rule? An independent experiment that uses a Jev Boolean judgment as the only logic primitive for gates, an SR latch, and Rule 110 cell updates, with recorded runs and a ground-truth checker. It is not affiliated with TypeSafe AI or Vercel.

item.title: Thread: AI Agent Journey Journal
item.description: How can a public journal describe the lasting changes in a personal AI-agent system without turning routine updates or private operating details into a story? A static, evidence-backed journal about changes from conversational AI assistants toward persistent local agent systems. It records directional changes in architecture, operation, governance, and understanding rather than routine updates.
